children: Short-term Bitcoin holders moved more than 113,000 BTC onto exchanges over a 48-hour stretch. Most of those coins arrived worth less than their owners paid for them.
The selling pressure came in waves rather than as one steady trickle. On November 3, short-term holders sent 50,790 BTC to exchanges, all of it carrying unrealized losses.
A week later, on November 10, another 46,060 BTC followed the same path. Those coins were also underwater when they moved.
By midnight UTC on November 11, roughly 47,025 BTC had been transferred to exchanges at a loss. That marks the third-highest reading since late July.
The balance between pain and profit was lopsided. Loss-making inflows outpaced profitable ones at a ratio of 27:1.
Combined inflows to major exchanges neared 48,500 BTC, worth about $3.6 billion, within a single 24-hour window. Binance drew a notable share of the activity.
On November 3, the exchange took in 8,114 BTC from coins that were between one day and one week old.
The average short-term holder's cost basis sits around $75,700.
Bitcoin dropped well under that level. On November 11, it touched an 11-week low of approximately $72,670.

Sending coins to an exchange does not guarantee a sale. However, it is usually the step investors take right before selling, which is why analysts treat exchange inflows as a gauge of potential selling pressure.
Over a 30-day period through mid-November, short-term holders sent about 706,000 BTC to the five largest exchanges.
Only around 2.5% of that volume arrived in profit. That is the third-lowest share recorded since 2021.

Short-term holders are generally the most price-sensitive group in the Bitcoin market. They bought recently, often near higher prices, and have less conviction than long-term holders who have sat through multiple cycles.
The 27:1 loss-to-profit ratio suggests sentiment among recent buyers remains fragile.
One level worth watching is the area around $73,000. Bitcoin already dipped below it on November 11, and a sustained failure to hold that zone could keep selling pressure elevated.
The $75,700 cost basis is the other line to track. A move back above it would put the average short-term holder back in profit, which tends to reduce the urge to dump coins.
A fresh surge in exchange inflows, especially from very young coins like the ones Binance absorbed on November 3, could signal that another wave of selling is building.

Long-term holders, by contrast, are not the ones driving this activity. The stress is concentrated among people who arrived late to the latest move, which is a familiar pattern in Bitcoin's corrections.

title: Short-term Bitcoin holders capitulate as over 113K BTC hits exchanges
